{{Short description|Type of group in mathematics}}
In the mathematical subject of [[group theory]], a '''one-relator group''' is a group given by a [[group presentation]] with a single defining relation. One-relator groups play an important role in [[geometric group theory]] by providing many explicit examples of finitely presented groups.

==Formal definition==

A one-relator group is a group ''G'' that admits a group presentation of the form

{{NumBlk|:|<math> G=\langle X\mid r=1\,  \rangle </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

where ''X'' is a set (in general possibly infinite), and where <math>r\in F(X)</math> is a freely and cyclically reduced word.

If ''Y'' is the set of all letters <math>x\in X</math> that appear in ''r'' and <math>X'=X\setminus Y</math> then 
:<math>G=\langle Y\mid  r=1\,  \rangle \ast F(X'). </math>

For that reason ''X'' in ({{EquationNote|1}}) is usually assumed to be finite where one-relator groups are discussed, in which case ({{EquationNote|1}}) can be rewritten more explicitly as

{{NumBlk|:|<math> G=\langle x_1,\dots, x_n\mid r=1\,  \rangle, </math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

where <math> X=\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}</math> for some integer <math>n\ge 1.</math>

==Freiheitssatz==
{{Main|Freiheitssatz}}

Let ''G'' be a one-relator group given by presentation ({{EquationNote|1}}) above. Recall that ''r'' is a freely and cyclically reduced word in ''F''(''X''). Let <math>y\in X</math> be a letter such that <math>y</math> or <math>y^{-1}</math> appears in ''r''. Let <math>X_1\subseteq X\setminus \{y\}</math>. The subgroup <math> H=\langle X_1\rangle\le G</math> is called a Magnus subgroup of ''G''. 

A famous 1930 theorem of [[Wilhelm Magnus]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Magnus |first1=Wilhelm |title=Über diskontinuierliche Gruppen mit einer definierenden Relation. (Der Freiheitssatz). |journal=[[Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik]] |date=1930 |volume=1930 |issue=163 |pages=141–165 |doi=10.1515/crll.1930.163.141|mr=1581238|s2cid=117245586 }}</ref> known as [[Freiheitssatz]], states that in this situation ''H'' is [[free group|freely generated by <math>X_1</math>]], that is, <math>H=F(X_1)</math>. See also<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Lyndon | first = Roger C. | author-link = Roger Lyndon
 | doi = 10.1112/jlms/s2-5.1.95
 | journal = [[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]]
 | mr = 0294465
 | pages = 95–101
 | series = Second Series
 | title = On the Freiheitssatz
 | volume = 5
 | year = 1972
 | hdl = 2027.42/135658
 | hdl-access = free
 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Weinbaum | first = C. M.
 | journal = Illinois Journal of Mathematics
 | mr = 0297849
 | pages = 308–322
 | title = On relators and diagrams for groups with one defining relation
 | volume = 16
 | year = 1972
 | issue = 2
 | doi = 10.1215/ijm/1256052287
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> for other proofs.

==Properties of one-relator groups==

Here we assume that a one-relator group ''G'' is given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}) with a finite generating set <math>X=\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}</math> and a nontrivial freely and cyclically reduced defining relation <math>1\ne r\in F(X)</math>.

*A one-relator group ''G'' is [[torsion-free group|torsion-free]] if and only if <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is not a proper power.

* Every one-relator group ''G''  is [[virtually]] torsion-free, that is, admits a torsion-free [[Index of a subgroup|subgroup of finite index]].<ref name=FKS>{{cite journal |last1=Fischer |first1=J. |last2=Karrass |first2=A. |last3=Solitar |first3=D. |title=On one-relator groups having elements of finite order |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1972 |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=297–301 |doi=10.2307/2038048|jstor=2038048 |mr=311780|doi-access=free}}</ref>

* Every one-relator group is coherent. <ref name=JZL>{{cite journal |last1=Jaikin-Zapirain |last2=Linton |first1=Andrei |first2=Marco |title=On the coherence of one-relator groups and their group algebras |journal=[[Annals of Mathematics]] |date=2025 |volume=201 |issue=3 |pages=909–959 |doi=10.4007/annals.2025.201.3.4|hdl=10261/425191 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>  That is, every finitely generated subgroup is finitely presented.

*A one-relator presentation is diagrammatically aspherical.<ref>Lyndon & Schupp, Ch. III, Section 11, Proposition 11.1, p. 161 </ref>

*If <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is not a proper power then the [[presentation complex]] ''P'' for presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}) is a finite [[Eilenberg–MacLane space|Eilenberg–MacLane complex]] <math>K(G,1)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dyer |first1=Eldon |last2=Vasquez |first2=A. T. |title=Some small aspherical spaces |journal=[[Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society]] |date=1973 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=332–352 |doi=10.1017/S1446788700015147|mr=0341476|doi-access=free }}</ref> 

*If <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is not a proper power then a one-relator group ''G''  has [[cohomological dimension]] <math>\le 2</math>.

* A one-relator group {{mvar|G}} is [[free group|free]] if and only if <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is a [[Primitive element (free group)|primitive element]] or the empty word; in the case of a primitive word {{mvar|G}} is free of rank {{math|''n''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1}}, in the case of the empty word it is free of rank {{mvar|n}}.<ref>Magnus, Karrass and Solitar, Theorem N3, p. 167 </ref>

*Suppose the element <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is of minimal length under the action of <math>\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)</math>, and suppose that for every <math>i=1,\dots,n</math> either <math>x_i</math> or <math>x_i^{-1}</math> occurs in ''r''. Then the group ''G'' is  [[Free product|freely indecomposable]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shenitzer |first1=Abe |title=Decomposition of a group with a single defining relation into a free product |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1955 |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=273–279 |doi=10.2307/2032354|jstor=2032354 |mr=69174|doi-access=free}}</ref>

*If <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is not a proper power then a one-relator group ''G''  is [[locally indicable group|locally indicable]], that is, every nontrivial finitely generated subgroup of ''G'' admits a [[group homomorphism]] onto <math>\mathbb Z</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Howie |first1=James |title=On locally indicable groups |journal=[[Mathematische Zeitschrift]] |date=1980 |volume=182 |issue=4 |pages=445–461 |doi=10.1007/BF01214717|mr=667000|s2cid=121292137 }}</ref>

*Every one-relator group ''G'' has algorithmically decidable [[Word problem for groups|word problem]].<ref name=WP>Magnus, Karrass and Solitar, Theorem 4.14, p. 274 </ref>

*If ''G'' is a one-relator group and <math>H\le G</math> is a Magnus subgroup then the [[subgroup membership problem]] for ''H'' in ''G'' is decidable.<ref name=WP/> 

* It is unknown if one-relator groups have solvable [[conjugacy problem]].

* It is unknown if the [[Group isomorphism problem|isomorphism problem]] is decidable for the class of one-relator groups.

* A one-relator group ''G'' given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}) has [[Rank of a group|rank]] ''n'' (that is, it cannot be generated by fewer than ''n'' elements) unless <math>r\in F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is a primitive element.<ref>Lyndon & Schupp, Ch. II, Section 5, Proposition 5.11 </ref>

* Let ''G'' be a one-relator group given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}). If <math>n\ge 3</math> then the [[Center (group theory)|center]] of ''G'' is trivial, <math>Z(G)=\{1\}</math>. If <math>n=2</math> and ''G'' is non-abelian with non-trivial center, then the center of ''G'' is [[infinite cyclic]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Murasugi |first1=Kunio |title=The center of a group with a single defining relation |journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]] |date=1964 |volume=155 |issue=3 |pages=246–251 |doi=10.1007/BF01344162|mr=163945|s2cid=119454184 }}</ref>

* Let <math>r,s\in F(X)</math> where <math>X=\{x_1,\dots, x_n\}</math>. Let <math>N_1=\langle\langle r\rangle\rangle_{F(X)}</math> and <math>N_2=\langle\langle s\rangle\rangle_{F(X)}</math> be the [[Normal closure (group theory)|normal closure]]s of ''r'' and ''s'' in ''F''(''X'') accordingly. Then <math>N_1=N_2</math> if and only if <math>r</math> is [[Conjugacy class|conjugate]] to <math>s</math> or <math>s^{-1}</math> in ''F''(''X'').<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Magnus |first1=Wilhelm |title=Untersuchungen über einige unendliche diskontinuierliche Gruppen |journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]] |date=1931 |volume=105 |issue=1 |pages=52–74 |doi=10.1007/BF01455808|mr=1512704|s2cid=120949491 }}</ref><ref>Lyndon & Schupp, p. 112 </ref>

*There exists a finitely generated one-relator group that is not [[Hopfian group|Hopfian]] and therefore not [[residually finite group|residually finite]], for example the [[Baumslag–Solitar group]] <math>B(2,3)=\langle a,b\mid b^{-1}a^2b=a^3\rangle</math>.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Gilbert Baumslag|author2=Donald Solitar|title=Some two-generator one-relator non-Hopfian groups|journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=68|year=1962|issue=3|pages=199–201|mr=0142635|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1962-10745-9|doi-access=free}} </ref>

* Let ''G'' be a one-relator group given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}). Then ''G'' satisfies the following version of the [[Tits alternative]]. If ''G'' is torsion-free then every subgroup of ''G'' either contains a free group of rank 2 or is [[solvable group|solvable]]. If ''G'' has nontrivial torsion, then every subgroup of ''G'' either contains a free group of rank 2, or is [[cyclic group|cyclic]], or is [[infinite dihedral group|infinite dihedral]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chebotarʹ |first1=A.A. |title=Subgroups of groups with one defining relation that do not contain free subgroups of rank 2 |journal=[[Algebra i Logika]] |date=1971 |volume=10 |issue=5 |pages=570–586 |url=http://math.nsc.ru/~alglog/01-10/10/10N5-8.pdf|mr=0313404}}</ref>

* Let ''G'' be a one-relator group given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}). Then the normal subgroup <math>N=\langle\langle r\rangle\rangle_{F(X)}\le F(X)</math> admits a free basis of the form <math>\{u_i^{-1}ru_i\mid i\in I\}</math> for some family of elements <math>\{u_i\in F(X)\mid i\in I\}</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=Daniel E. |last2=Lyndon |first2=Roger C. |title=Free bases for normal subgroups of free groups |journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1963 |volume=108 |issue=3 |pages=526–537 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1963-0170930-9|mr=0170930|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==One-relator groups with torsion==

Suppose a one-relator group ''G'' given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}) where <math>r=s^m</math> where <math>m\ge 2</math> and where <math>1\ne s\in F(X)</math> is not a proper power (and thus ''s'' is also freely and cyclically reduced). Then the following hold:

* The element ''s'' has [[Order (group theory)|order]] ''m'' in ''G'', and every element of finite order in ''G'' is conjugate to a power of ''s''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Karrass |first1=A. |last2=Magnus |first2=W. |last3=Solitar |first3=D. |title=Elements of finite order in groups with a single defining relation |journal=[[Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics]] |date=1960 |volume=13 |pages=57–66 |doi=10.1002/cpa.3160130107|mr=124384}}</ref>

* Every finite subgroup of ''G'' is [[Conjugate subgroup|conjugate]] to a subgroup of <math>\langle s\rangle </math> in ''G''.  Moreover, the subgroup of ''G'' generated by all torsion elements is a free product of a family of conjugates of <math>\langle s\rangle </math> in ''G''.<ref name=FKS/>

* ''G'' admits a torsion-free [[normal subgroup]] of finite index.<ref name=FKS/>

* Newman's "spelling theorem"<ref name=Newman>{{cite journal |last1=Newman |first1=B. B. |title=Some results on one-relator groups |journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] |date=1968 |volume=74 |issue=3 |pages=568–571 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1968-12012-9|mr=222152|doi-access=free|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society/volume-74/issue-3/Some-results-on-one-relator-groups/bams/1183529638.pdf }}</ref><ref>Lyndon & Schupp, Ch. IV, Theorem 5.5, p. 205 </ref> Let <math>1\ne w\in F(X)</math> be a freely reduced word such that <math>w=1</math> in ''G''. Then ''w'' contains a subword ''v'' such that ''v'' is also a subword of <math>r</math> or <math>r^{-1}</math> of length <math>|v|=1+(m-1)|s|</math>. Since <math>m\ge 2</math> that means that <math>|v|>|r|/2</math> and presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}) of ''G'' is a [[Dehn's algorithm|Dehn presentation]].

* ''G'' has virtual cohomological dimension  <math>\le 2</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Howie |first1=James |title=Cohomology of one-relator products of locally indicable groups |journal=[[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]] |date=1984 |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=419–430 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s2-30.3.419|mr=810951}}</ref>

* ''G'' is a [[word-hyperbolic group]].<ref name=BFR>{{cite book |last1=Baumslag |first1=Gilbert |last2=Fine |first2=Benjamin |last3=Rosenberger |first3=Gerhard |title=Groups St Andrews 2017 in Birmingham |date=2019 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-72874-4 |pages=119–157 |chapter=One-relator groups: an overview|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mkaPDwAAQBAJ&dq=one-relator+groups+with+torsion+are+word-hyperbolic&pg=PA136|mr=3931411|series=London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Ser.|volume=455}}</ref>

* ''G'' has decidable [[conjugacy problem]].<ref name=Newman/>

* ''G'' is [[coherent group|coherent]], that is every finitely generated subgroup of ''G'' is finitely presentable.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Louder |first1=Larsen |last2=Wilton |first2=Henry |title=One-relator groups with torsion are coherent |journal=Mathematical Research Letters |date=2020 |volume=27 |issue=5 |pages=1499–1512 |doi=10.4310/MRL.2020.v27.n5.a9|arxiv=1805.11976 |mr=4216595|s2cid=119141737 }}</ref>

* The [[Group isomorphism problem|isomorphism problem]] is decidable for finitely generated one-relator groups with torsion, by virtue of their hyperbolicity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dahmani |first1=Francois |last2=Guirardel |first2=Vincent |title=The isomorphism problem for all hyperbolic groups |journal=[[Geometric and Functional Analysis]] |date=2011 |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=223–300 |doi=10.1007/s00039-011-0120-0|mr=2795509|doi-access=free|arxiv=1002.2590 }}</ref>

* ''G'' is [[residually finite group|residually finite]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wise |first1=Daniel T. |title=Research announcement: the structure of groups with a quasiconvex hierarchy |journal=Electronic Research Announcements in Mathematical Sciences |date=2009 |volume=16 |pages=44–55 |doi=10.3934/era.2009.16.44|mr=2558631|doi-access=free}}</ref>

* <math>G</math> is virtually [[free-by-cyclic group|free-by-cyclic]], i.e. <math>G</math> has a subgroup <math>H</math> of finite-index such that there is a free normal subgroup <math>F \triangleleft H</math> with cyclic quotient <math>F/H</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kielak |first1=Dawid |last2=Linton |first2=Marco |title=Virtually free-by-cyclic groups |journal=Geometric and Functional Analysis |date=2024 |volume=34 |pages=1580-1608 |doi=10.1007/s00039-024-00687-6|mr=4792841|doi-access=free|arxiv=2302.11500 }}</ref>

==Magnus–Moldavansky method==

Starting with the work of Magnus in the 1930s, most general results about one-relator groups are proved by induction on the length |''r''| of the defining relator ''r''. 
The presentation below follows Section 6 of Chapter II of Lyndon and Schupp<ref>Lyndon& Schupp, Chapter II, Section 6, pp. 111-113</ref> and Section 4.4 of Magnus, Karrass and Solitar<ref>Magnus, Karrass, and Solitar, Section 4.4 </ref> for Magnus' original approach and Section 5 of Chapter IV of Lyndon and Schupp<ref>Lyndon& Schupp, Chapter IV, Section 5, pp. 198-205</ref> for the Moldavansky's HNN-extension version of that approach.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Moldavanskii |first1=D.I. |title=Certain subgroups of groups with one defining relation |journal=[[Siberian Mathematical Journal]] |date=1967 |volume=8 |pages=1370–1384|doi=10.1007/BF02196411 |mr=0220810|s2cid=119585707 }}</ref>

Let ''G'' be a one-relator group given by presentation ({{EquationNote|1}}) with a finite generating set ''X''. Assume also that every generator from ''X'' actually occurs in ''r''.

One can usually assume that <math>\#X\ge 2</math> (since otherwise ''G'' is cyclic and whatever statement is being proved about ''G'' is usually obvious). 

The main case to consider when some generator, say ''t'', from ''X'' occurs in ''r'' with exponent sum 0 on ''t''. Say <math> X=\{t, a, b,\dots, z\}</math> in this case. For every generator <math>x\in X\setminus \{t\}</math> one denotes <math>x_i=t^{-i}xt^i</math> where <math>i\in \mathbb Z</math>. Then ''r'' can be rewritten as a word <math>r_0</math> in these new generators <math>X_{\infty}= \{(a_i)_i, (b_i)_i, \dots, (z_i)_i\}</math> with <math>|r_0|<|r|</math>.

For example, if <math>r=t^{-2}bt a t^3b^{-2}a^2t^{-1}at^{-1}</math> then <math>r_0=b_2a_1b_{-2}^{-2}a_{-2}^2a_{-1}</math>.

Let <math>X_0</math> be the alphabet consisting of the portion of <math>X_{\infty}</math> given by all <math>x_i</math> with <math>m(x)\le i\le M(x)</math> where <math>m(x), M(x)</math> are the minimum and the maximum subscripts with which <math>x_i^{\pm 1}</math> occurs in <math>r_0</math>.

Magnus observed that the subgroup <math>L=\langle X_0\rangle \le G</math> is itself a one-relator group with the one-relator presentation <math>L=\langle X_0\mid r_0=1\rangle</math>. Note that since <math>|r_0|<|r|</math>, one can usually apply the inductive hypothesis to <math>L</math> when proving a particular statement about ''G''.

Moreover, if <math>X_i=t^{-i}X_0t^i</math> for <math>i\in \mathbb Z</math> then <math>L_i=\langle X_i\rangle=\langle X_i| r_i=1\rangle</math> is also a one-relator group, where <math>r_i</math> is obtained from <math>r_0</math> by shifting all subscripts by <math>i</math>. Then the normal closure <math> N=\langle \langle X_0\rangle\rangle_G</math> of <math>X_0</math> in ''G'' is
:<math>N=\left\langle \bigcup_{i\in \mathbb Z} L_i \right\rangle. </math>

Magnus' original approach exploited the fact that ''N'' is actually an iterated [[amalgamated product]] of the groups <math>L_i</math>, amalgamated along suitably chosen Magnus free subgroups. His proof of [[Freiheitssatz]] and of the solution of the word problem for one-relator groups was based on this approach.

Later Moldavansky simplified the framework and noted that in this case ''G'' itself is an [[HNN-extension]] of ''L'' with associated subgroups being Magnus free subgroups of ''L''.

If for every generator from <math>X_0</math> its minimum and maximum subscripts in <math>r_0</math> are equal then <math>G=L\ast \langle t\rangle</math> and the inductive step is usually easy to handle in this case.

Suppose then that some generator from <math>X_0</math> occurs in <math>r_0</math> with at least two distinct subscripts. We put <math>Y_-</math> to be the set of all generators from <math>X_0</math> with non-maximal subscripts and we put <math>Y_+</math> to be the set of all generators from <math>X_0</math> with non-maximal subscripts. (Hence every generator from <math>Y_-</math> and from <math>Y_-</math> occurs in <math>r_0</math> with a non-unique subscript.) Then <math>H_-=\langle Y_-\rangle</math> and <math>H_+=\langle Y_+\rangle</math> are free Magnus subgroups of ''L'' and <math>t^{-1}H_- t=H_+</math>. Moldavansky observed that in this situation 
:<math>G=\langle L, t\mid t^{-1}H_- t=H_+\rangle </math>
is an HNN-extension of ''L''. This fact often allows proving something about ''G'' using the inductive hypothesis about the one-relator group ''L'' via the use of normal form methods and structural algebraic properties for the HNN-extension ''G''.

The general case, both in Magnus' original setting and in Moldavansky's simplification of it, requires treating the situation where no generator from ''X'' occurs with exponent sum 0 in ''r''. Suppose that distinct letters <math>x,y\in X</math> occur in ''r'' with nonzero exponents <math>\alpha, \beta</math> accordingly. Consider a homomorphism <math>f:F(X)\to F(X)</math> given by <math>f(x)=xy^{-\beta}, f(y)=y^\alpha</math> and fixing the other generators from ''X''. Then for <math>r'=f(r)\in F(X)</math> the exponent sum on ''y'' is equal to 0. The map ''f'' induces a [[group homomorphism]] <math>\phi: G\to G'=\langle X\mid r'=1\rangle</math> that turns out to be an embedding.
The one-relator group ''G''' can then be treated using Moldavansky's approach. When <math>G'</math> splits as an HNN-extension of a one-relator group ''L'', the defining relator <math>r_0</math> of ''L'' still turns out to be shorter than ''r'', allowing for inductive arguments to proceed. Magnus' original approach used a similar version of an embedding trick for dealing with this case.

==Two-generator one-relator groups==

It turns out that many two-generator one-relator groups split as [[semidirect product]]s <math>G=F_m\rtimes\mathbb Z</math>. This fact was observed by [[Kenneth Brown (mathematician)|Ken Brown]] when analyzing the BNS-invariant of one-relator groups using the Magnus-Moldavansky method.

Namely, let ''G'' be a one-relator group given by presentation ({{EquationNote|2}}) with <math>n=2</math> and let <math>\phi:G\to \mathbb Z</math> be an epimorphism. One can then change a free basis of <math>F(X)</math> to a basis <math>t,a</math> such that <math>\phi(t)=1,\phi(a)=0</math> and rewrite the presentation of ''G'' in this generators as
:<math>G=\langle a,t\mid r=1\rangle </math>
where <math>1\ne r=r(a,t)\in F(a,t)</math> is a freely and cyclically reduced word.

Since <math>\phi(r)=0, \phi(t)=1</math>, the exponent sum on ''t'' in ''r'' is equal to 0. Again putting <math>a_i=t^{-i}at^i</math>, we can rewrite ''r'' as a word <math>r_0</math> in <math>(a_i)_{i\in \mathbb Z}.</math> Let <math>m,M</math> be the minimum and the maximum subscripts of the generators occurring in <math>r_0</math>. Brown showed<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Kenneth S. |title=Trees, valuations, and the Bieri-Neumann-Strebel invariant |journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]] |date=1987 |volume=90 |issue=3 |pages=479–504 |doi=10.1007/BF01389176|bibcode=1987InMat..90..479B |mr=0914847|s2cid=122703100 }}, Theorem 4.3</ref> that <math>\ker(\phi)</math> is finitely generated [[if and only if]] <math>m<M</math> and both <math>a_m</math> and <math>a_{M}</math> occur exactly once in <math>r_0</math>, and moreover, in that case the group <math>\ker(\phi)</math> is free.
Therefore if <math>\phi:G\to \mathbb Z</math> is an epimorphism with a finitely generated kernel, then ''G'' splits as <math>G=F_m\rtimes \mathbb Z</math> where <math>F_m=\ker(\phi)</math> is a finite rank [[free group]]. 

Later Dunfield and Thurston proved<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dunfield |first1=Nathan |last2=Thurston |first2=Dylan |title=A random tunnel number one 3–manifold does not fiber over the circle |journal=[[Geometry & Topology]] |date=2006 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=2431–2499 |arxiv=math/0510129|doi=10.2140/gt.2006.10.2431|doi-access=free|mr=2284062}}, Theorem 6.1</ref> that if a one-relator two-generator group <math>G=\langle x_1,x_2\mid r=1\rangle</math> is chosen "at random" (that is, a cyclically reduced word ''r'' of length ''n'' in <math>F(x_1,x_2)</math> is chosen uniformly at random) then the probability <math>p_n</math> that a homomorphism from ''G'' onto  <math>\mathbb Z</math> with a finitely generated kernel exists satisfies
:<math> 0.0006<p_n<0.975</math>
for all sufficiently large ''n''. Moreover, their experimental data indicates that the limiting value for <math>p_n</math> is close to <math>0.94</math>.

==Examples of one-relator groups==

* [[Free abelian group]] <math> \mathbb Z\times \mathbb Z=\langle a, b \mid a^{-1}b^{-1}ab=1\rangle</math> 

* [[Baumslag–Solitar group]] <math> B(m, n)=\langle a,b\mid b^{-1} a^m b= a^n\rangle</math> where <math> m,n\ne 0</math>.

* [[Torus knot]] group <math> G=\langle a, b\mid a^p=b^q\rangle</math> where <math>p,q\ge 1</math> are [[coprime integers]].

* [[Baumslag–Gersten group]] <math> G=\langle a,t \mid a^{a^t}=a^2\rangle =\langle a, t \mid (t^{-1}a^{-1}t) a (t^{-1} at)=a^2 \rangle  </math>

* Oriented [[surface group]] <math> G=\langle a_1, b_1, \dots, a_n, b_n\mid [a_1,b_1]\dots [a_n,b_n]=1\rangle</math> where <math>[a,b]=a^{-1}b^{-1}ab</math> and where <math> n\ge 1</math>.

* Non-oriented surface group <math> G=\langle a_1,\dots, a_n\mid a_1^2\cdots a_n^2=1\rangle</math>, where <math>n\ge 1</math>.

==Generalizations and open problems==

*If ''A'' and ''B'' are two groups, and <math>r\in A\ast B</math> is an element in their [[free product]], one can consider a '''one-relator product''' <math>G=A\ast B/\langle\langle r\rangle\rangle=\langle A, B\mid r=1\rangle</math>.

*The so-called Kervaire conjecture, also known as Kervaire–Laudenbach conjecture, asks if it is true that if ''A'' is a nontrivial group and <math>B=\langle t\rangle</math> is infinite cyclic then for every <math>r\in A\ast B</math> the one-relator product <math>G=\langle A, t\mid r=1\rangle</math> is nontrivial.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gersten |first1=S. M. |title=Combinatorial group theory and topology (Alta, Utah, 1984) |date=1987 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=0-691-08409-2 |pages=121–144 |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781400882083-007/pdf |chapter=Nonsingular equations of small weight over groups|series=Annals of Mathematics Studies|volume=111|doi=10.1515/9781400882083-007 |mr=0895612}}</ref>

*Klyachko proved the Kervaire conjecture for the case where ''A'' is torsion-free.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Klyachko |first1=A. A. |title=A funny property of sphere and equations over groups |journal=[[Communications in Algebra]] |date=1993 |volume=21 |issue=7 |pages=2555–2575 |doi=10.1080/00927879308824692|mr=1218513}}</ref>

*A conjecture attributed to Gersten<ref name=BFR/> says that a finitely generated one-relator group is word-hyperbolic if and only if it contains no Baumslag–Solitar subgroups.
